title: Faulty Comparisons
kicker: American Diploma · ACT · English: Conventions of Standard English
summary: Compare like with like — that of / those of, possessive fixes, like/unlike openers, "than any other" and comparison forms, with four worked items and two ACT-style practice essays.

blocks.text: What this question type tests

Faulty-comparison questions belong to the **Conventions of Standard English** reporting category of the ACT English test (38–43% of the English score, together with punctuation, usage and the other sentence-structure skills). The English test has **50 questions (40 scored) in 35 minutes**, over five essays: three of about 340 words with 10 questions each and two of about 185 words with 5 questions each.

As with every ACT English item, a part of the essay is **underlined** and numbered, and you choose the best of four versions (the first is usually **NO CHANGE**). You know a comparison item is in front of you when the choices add or remove words such as **that of, those of, 's, other, than/then, more/most, -er/-est**, or when they reorder the words after *like* or *unlike*.

The core rule: **a comparison must compare two things of the same kind.** A population with a population, a city with a city, one writer's style with another writer's style. Everyday speech is often careless ("My phone is better than yours" is fine, but "My phone's camera is better than you" is not), and the ACT turns that carelessness into wrong answers. The sentence often *sounds* fine — that is exactly why these questions are hard.

blocks.title: الفكرة الأساسية
blocks.text: المقارنة لازم تكون بين حاجتين من نفس النوع: عدد سكان مع عدد سكان، مدينة مع مدينة، مقال مع مقال. اسأل نفسك: إيه الحاجتين اللي بنقارنهم بالظبط؟ لو واحدة شيء والتانية شخص أو مكان، المقارنة غلط.
Rule 1: Name the two things being compared

Before you look at the choices, say the two things in your own words. Ask: "**What** is bigger / older / better than **what**?" The first thing is usually the subject; the second comes after *than*, *as*, *like*, *unlike*, *similar to*, *different from* or *compared with*.

rows: Quality vs place
The climate of Aswan is drier than Alexandria.
The climate of Aswan is drier than that of Alexandria.
Possession vs owner
Salma's handwriting is neater than her brother.
Salma's handwriting is neater than her brother's.
Part vs whole
The roof of the new school is higher than the old school.
The roof of the new school is higher than that of the old school.
Work vs person
The novels of Naguib Mahfouz are longer than most writers.
The novels of Naguib Mahfouz are longer than those of most writers.
Action vs person
Cycling to work is faster than my neighbour.
Cycling to work is faster than my neighbour's daily drive.
Group vs individual
Like a doctor, a nurse's training takes years.
Like a doctor's training, a nurse's training takes years.

blocks.text: Rule 2: The three standard fixes — that of, those of, 's
When the second thing in a comparison is missing, the ACT repairs it in one of three ways. All three are correct; choose the one the choices offer, and check that it fits grammatically.

items: **that of** — replaces a **singular** noun: "The population of Egypt is larger than **that of** Canada." (that = the population)
**those of** — replaces a **plural** noun: "The pyramids of Giza are older than **those of** Mexico." (those = the pyramids)
**possessive 's** — the noun is understood after it: "Egypt's population is larger than **Canada's**." (Canada's = Canada's population)
**repeat the noun** — always safe, sometimes wordy: "Egypt's population is larger than Canada's population."

blocks.text: **Match the number.** *That* must point back to a singular noun and *those* to a plural noun. This is where many careful students lose the point:

items: ✗ The streets of the old city are narrower than **that** of the new suburbs. (streets = plural)
✓ The streets of the old city are narrower than **those** of the new suburbs.
✗ The temperature in July is higher than **those** in January. (temperature = singular)
✓ The temperature in July is higher than **that** in January.

blocks.text: **Prepositions can also fix a comparison.** When the first thing is "X *in* a place" or "X *at* a time", repeating the preposition is enough: "Rainfall in Alexandria is higher **than in** Aswan." "Prices this year are lower **than in** 2024." Without the preposition, the comparison breaks: ✗ "Rainfall in Alexandria is higher than Aswan."

**Possessive pronouns** work the same way: *mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs*. ✗ "Her score was higher than **me**." (score vs person) → ✓ "Her score was higher than **mine**." Note that "She scored higher than **I** (did)" is also correct — there the two people are compared, because the verb *scored* is the action.
Rule 3: Like, unlike, similar to — the noun after the comma

A sentence that opens with *Like …*, *Unlike …*, *Similar to …* or *As with …* compares the noun in that phrase with the **subject that comes right after the comma**. The two must be the same kind of thing. This works exactly like a dangling modifier, and it is one of the ACT's favourite traps.

items: ✗ **Unlike** most desert plants, **the leaves** of the acacia stay green in summer. (plants vs leaves)
✓ **Unlike** most desert plants, **the acacia** stays green in summer.
✓ **Unlike** the leaves of most desert plants, **the leaves** of the acacia stay green in summer.
✗ **Like** his father, **Ahmed's career** began in a small workshop. (father vs career)
✓ **Like** his father, **Ahmed** began his career in a small workshop.
✓ **Like** his father's career, **Ahmed's career** began in a small workshop.

blocks.text: **The possessive trap:** "Like many coastal towns, **Rashid's** economy depends on fishing." The subject is not Rashid; it is *economy*. A town is being compared with an economy. Fix: "Like many coastal towns, Rashid depends on fishing."

blocks.title: that of و those of
blocks.text: لو الحاجة اللي بتقارنها مفرد استخدم that of، ولو جمع استخدم those of. أو استخدم 's: Egypt's population is larger than Canada's. وفي جمل Like / Unlike: الاسم اللي بعد الفاصلة لازم يكون من نفس نوع الاسم اللي بعد Like.
Rule 4: "Than any other" — do not compare something with itself

When you compare one member of a group with the rest of the group, add **other** (or **else** with *anyone, anything, anybody*). Without it, the sentence compares the thing with itself, which is illogical.

items: ✗ Mount Catherine is higher than **any mountain** in Egypt. (it is a mountain in Egypt — higher than itself?)
✓ Mount Catherine is higher than **any other mountain** in Egypt.
✗ Mona finished the race faster than **anyone** on her team.
✓ Mona finished the race faster than **anyone else** on her team.
✓ The Nile is longer than **any river** in Europe. (no *other* needed — the Nile is not in Europe)

blocks.text: You can combine Rule 4 with Rule 2: "His descriptions are more detailed than **those of any other** keeper." Descriptions vs descriptions (those of), and the keeper is not compared with himself (other).
Rule 5: Correct comparison forms
Some items test the form of the comparing word rather than the logic. These are quick points if you know them.

rows: Two things → -er / more; three or more → -est / most
Of the two plans, the second is the best.
Of the two plans, the second is the better.
Never double: more + -er, most + -est
This road is more safer at night.
This road is safer at night.
Irregular forms
Her second novel is more good than the first.
Her second novel is better than the first.
than (comparison) vs then (time)
The bus is cheaper then the train.
The bus is cheaper than the train.
as … as (never as … than)
The library is as quiet than a mosque at dawn.
The library is as quiet as a mosque at dawn.
different from (ACT standard)
City life is very different than village life.
City life is very different from village life.
fewer (countable) vs less (amount)
Less students attended this year.
Fewer students attended this year.

blocks.text: Rule 6: Illogical, unclear and incomplete comparisons

**Ambiguous comparisons.** "Nour trusts her coach more than her teammates." Does Nour trust the coach more than she trusts her teammates, or more than her teammates trust the coach? Add the missing verb or pronoun: "…more than her teammates **do**" or "…more than **she trusts** her teammates."

**Doubled comparison words.** Use one comparing structure, not two: ✗ "Compared with last year, sales were higher **than before**." → ✓ "Sales were higher **than last year's**." or ✓ "Compared with last year, sales rose."

**Comparison with a missing second half.** "The new bridge is wider." Wider than what? On the ACT this is acceptable only if the previous sentence already names the other thing ("The old bridge had two lanes. The new bridge is wider."). Read the sentence before the underline.
**Comparing the wrong time.** "This year's harvest was larger than last year." A harvest is compared with a year. → ✓ "…than last year's." / ✓ "…than the harvest of last year."
A 4-step method for comparison items

items: **Find the comparison signal:** than, as … as, like, unlike, similar to, different from, compared with, more/most, -er/-est.
**Name thing 1 and thing 2** in plain words ("the price … bananas").
**Ask: same kind?** If not, look for the choice with *that of / those of / 's / in*, or the choice that changes the subject after *Like/Unlike*. Check singular vs plural for that/those.
**Check the extras:** *other/else* for a member of its own group; than not then; -er for two, -est for three or more; no *more + -er*.

blocks.text: Worked examples
**Worked example 1 — a missing "in" / "that of"**
Passage: Because the city lies on the Mediterranean, the winter rainfall in Alexandria is much higher __than Aswan__, where rain may not fall for years.
**Choose the best version of the underlined portion.**

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) than in Aswan
C) than those of Aswan
D) then in Aswan

blocks.text: **Answer: B**

items: A) ✗ Wrong: Compares rainfall with a city.
B) ✓ Correct: *Rainfall in Alexandria … than in Aswan* — rainfall compared with rainfall; the repeated *in* brings back the missing noun.
C) ✗ Wrong: *Those* is plural, but *rainfall* is singular.
D) ✗ Wrong: *Then* is a time word, not a comparison word.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2 — than any other**
Passage: At 2,629 metres, Mount Catherine in South Sinai is higher __than any mountain__ in Egypt.
**Choose the best version of the underlined portion.**

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) then any other mountain
C) than any other mountain
D) than all the mountains

blocks.text: **Answer: C**

items: A) ✗ Wrong: Mount Catherine is itself a mountain in Egypt, so without *other* it is compared with itself.
B) ✗ Wrong: Adds *other* but uses *then* (time) instead of *than*.
C) ✓ Correct: *Than any other mountain* compares it with the rest of the group, not with itself.
D) ✗ Wrong: *All the mountains* in Egypt still includes Mount Catherine — the same illogical comparison.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3 — unlike + the subject after the comma**
Passage: __Unlike most smartphones, the battery of this model__ can be replaced at home with a simple screwdriver.
**Choose the best version of the underlined portion.**

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) Unlike the batteries of most smartphones, the battery of this model
C) Unlike that of most smartphones, this model
D) Unlike most smartphones, this model's battery

blocks.text: **Answer: B**

items: A) ✗ Wrong: Compares smartphones with a battery.
B) ✓ Correct: Batteries compared with a battery — the same kind of thing on both sides of the comma.
C) ✗ Wrong: *That of* has no clear noun to point back to (it comes before the noun it replaces), and the subject is now *this model* — a model compared with a battery.
D) ✗ Wrong: Possessive trap: the subject is *battery*, not *model*, so phones are still compared with a battery.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4 — possessive pronoun**
Passage: Omar's sketches of the old Cairo streets are far more detailed __than me__, so the teacher asked him to draw the class poster.
**Choose the best version of the underlined portion.**

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) than mine
C) than I
D) than my

blocks.text: **Answer: B**

items: A) ✗ Wrong: Sketches compared with a person.
B) ✓ Correct: *Mine* = my sketches. Sketches are compared with sketches.
C) ✗ Wrong: *Than I* compares Omar's sketches with a person; it would only work for "Omar draws better than I (do)."
D) ✗ Wrong: *My* must be followed by a noun (my sketches); alone it is ungrammatical.

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **The sounds-fine comparison:** "The population of Alexandria is smaller than Cairo." People say it every day — it is still population vs city.
**The wrong-number fix:** *that of* for a plural noun or *those of* for a singular one.
**The possessive subject after Like/Unlike:** "Like many birds, the falcon's eyesight…" — the subject is *eyesight*.
**The missing *other*:** "better than any student in the class" when the person is in the class.
**than/then swap:** a choice with the perfect logic but *then* instead of *than*.
**The half-fix:** a choice that repairs the comparison but adds a tense or agreement error.
**Double comparatives:** more faster, most best, more better.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: Whenever you see *than*, *as … as*, *like* or *unlike*, stop and name the two things being compared.
Choices that add *that of*, *those of* or *'s* are a strong signal that the test-maker is checking comparison logic.
Check number: singular → *that*, plural → *those*.
After *Like/Unlike …,* the very next noun is the subject being compared — ignore possessive names in front of it.
In a comparison within a group, look for *other* or *else*.
If the original already compares like with like, choose NO CHANGE.

blocks.text: Practice

Two short ACT-style essays with five questions each. Every question refers to the numbered underlined portion. All ten items test comparisons; some wrong choices also contain errors from earlier lessons.

blocks.title: Faulty Comparisons — ACT-style practice
blocks.intro: Two essays, 10 questions. Choose the best version of each underlined portion. NO CHANGE keeps the original. Explanations appear after you answer.

questions.p:
Two Breakfasts, One Table

In many Egyptian homes, Friday breakfast means two dishes: ful medames and ta'ameya. Both are made from fava beans, yet the way ful is cooked is very different [1] __from ta'ameya__. Ful is simmered slowly for hours until the beans are soft, while ta'ameya is made from raw beans that are soaked, ground with fresh herbs, and fried in hot oil.

My grandfather has strong opinions about both. He insists that his ful is better [2] __than any other cook__ in our neighbourhood, and nobody in the family dares to disagree. My aunt, however, prefers ta'ameya. She says its crunchy outside is more satisfying [3] __than the soft texture of ful__.

The two dishes are also eaten differently. Ta'ameya tastes best straight from the pan, so it must be eaten [4] __more sooner__ than ful, which stays good in its pot for hours.

Last Friday, we held a family vote. Ta'ameya won by a single vote, so this year's contest was closer [5] __than last year__, when ful won easily. My grandfather was not pleased with the result. He has already announced a rematch for next Friday and has promised to cook his best pot of ful yet.
questions.q: Question 1: Choose the best version of underlined portion [1]. (NO CHANGE keeps it as it is.)
c: from the way ta'ameya is prepared
questions.e: The sentence compares *the way ful is cooked* with *the way ta'ameya is prepared* — a method with a method. A and C compare a method with a food (and C uses *different than*); D uses *different than* and leaves the comparison unfinished.

questions.e: This year's contest is compared with last year's (contest). A compares a contest with a year; C uses *then*; D uses plural *those* for the singular *contest*.

questions.p:
Built for the Sand

The fennec fox of the Sahara looks almost like a cartoon. Its body is smaller than [6] __a house cat__, but its ears can grow to about fifteen centimetres long. Relative to its body size, the fennec's ears are larger than [7] __those of any other member__ of the dog family. At night, the fox turns them slowly from side to side, listening for insects and small animals moving under the sand.

Those ears do more than hear. Blood flowing through them releases heat, so a fennec stays cooler in the desert sun [8] __than a red fox's__ in the same place. Its fur is also unusual. Unlike [9] __the paws of most foxes, thick hair covers the fennec's paws__, protecting them from the burning sand.

Food is hard to find in the desert, so the fennec cannot be a fussy eater. [10] __Like the red fox, the fennec's diet includes__ almost anything: insects, small rodents, eggs, and even roots and fruits that hold water. In a place where rain may not fall for months, such flexibility can mean the difference between surviving and starving.
questions.q: Question 6: Choose the best version of underlined portion [6]. (NO CHANGE keeps it as it is.)
questions.e: The fox's body is compared with a cat's body: *that of a house cat* (singular *body*). A and D compare a body with a whole animal; B uses plural *those* for a singular noun.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Compare like with like: name the two things and make sure they are the same kind.
Fix a broken comparison with *that of* (singular), *those of* (plural), *'s*, or a repeated preposition (*than in*).
After *Like / Unlike …,* the noun right after the comma is what is being compared — watch for possessives.
A member of its own group needs *other* / *else*: "than any other mountain in Egypt".
Two things → -er/more; three or more → -est/most; never *more + -er*; *than* not *then*; *as … as*.
